name: Testosterone cypionate

lead: Testosterone cypionate is a slow-release injectable ester of testosterone used to treat low testosterone and in masculinizing hormone therapy. Its labelled virilizing effects include deeper voice, body and facial hair growth, and acne.

The ester is released slowly and converted to testosterone, which activates the androgen receptor, including in laryngeal tissue. Voice change is a side effect of androgen action rather than a studied purpose, and no trials test it for appearance goals. Non-medical use for physique and performance is reported as common.

paras: Clinically it is prescribed for confirmed deficiency or gender-affirming care under medical supervision with regular monitoring. Effects such as body-composition and voice changes develop gradually over months.

Labelled risks include acne, hair loss, fertility suppression, cardiovascular events, clotting, polycythemia concerns and contraindication in pregnancy. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, and voice changes in women may be permanent.

angle.text: Testosterone cypionate is a long-acting injectable labelled for hypogonadism, and its androgen action on the larynx deepens the voice. That deepening is a listed virilizing effect rather than a studied purpose.

lead: Testosterone cypionate is a long-acting injectable ester of testosterone, sold mainly as Depo-Testosterone, that the body converts to testosterone after injection. It is FDA-labelled for replacement therapy in males with primary or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and it is also used in masculinizing hormone therapy for transgender men.[1][2][3]

In appearance terms, testosterone drives several visible traits: facial and body hair, a deeper voice, muscle mass and skin oiliness. The label lists acne, body and facial hair growth and voice deepening among its virilizing effects, and people in physique communities describe using it to build muscle, which they associate with a fuller, more muscular look.[1][3] Transgender men use it for the explicitly intended purpose of developing male secondary sexual characteristics such as a lower voice, facial hair and a more masculine fat and muscle distribution.[4]

Controlled trials have studied it in hypogonadal older men, in healthy men given supraphysiologic doses to examine mood and aggression, and in prostate cancer protocols. No trial has tested it for cosmetic goals in people with normal hormone levels. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States.[1][5][6]
infobox: About 7 to 8 days after intramuscular injection[1]
US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV[1]
UK Class C; prescription-only in the EU; WADA-banned [9]

paras: The US label lists replacement therapy in men with symptoms of testosterone deficiency. Covered conditions include primary hypogonadism (testicular failure from causes such as cryptorchidism, orchitis or orchidectomy) and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (gonadotropin or LHRH deficiency, or pituitary-hypothalamic injury).[3] A 1984 review described long-acting testosterone esters, enanthate and cypionate, as the standard injectable approach to adult male testosterone deficiency.[7]

It is also used off-label for other conditions, including masculinizing hormone therapy in transgender men. A Brazilian review of recommendations for transgender men reports that intramuscular testosterone esters are the most common formulation, with testosterone cypionate and enanthate widely used, and that male physical characteristics appear in nearly all users within about six months, with maximum virilization taking longer.[4]

The listed androgenic effects include growth of facial and body hair, voice deepening, acne, seborrhea and male-pattern hair loss.[1][3] Wikipedia notes that non-medical use for physique enhancement is common and that the drug is marketed mainly in the United States.[1]

Grokipedia's overview describes lean mass, strength and bone density gains as expected effects of androgen replacement in hypogonadal men.[2] Randomized data on these outcomes in older hypogonadal men come from a 12-month trial (see Clinical studies).[8]

Testosterone acts through the androgen receptor in muscle, skin, hair follicles and the larynx, so its visible effects fall in several areas. Wikipedia's overview of testosterone medication lists increased body and facial hair, possible scalp hair loss that 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride can reduce, oily skin, acne and seborrhea.[9] The same overview notes that in transgender men, injectable esters including cypionate are used for masculinizing effects.[9][4]

For muscle, the best-known controlled data come from a 1996 New England Journal of Medicine trial in 43 healthy men, who received supraphysiologic testosterone enanthate or placebo for 10 weeks with or without weight training. Testosterone without exercise raised triceps area by 424 mm2 versus a 81 mm2 fall on placebo and quadriceps area by 607 versus a 131 mm2 fall, with fat-free mass gains of 6.1 kg in the testosterone-plus-exercise group; mood and behavior did not change in any group.[10] That study used enanthate, which Wikipedia describes as essentially interchangeable with cypionate in its pharmacokinetic profile.[1]
Physique and looks communities discuss further appearance goals, including jaw definition and facial hair.[11] No controlled trial was found measuring facial bone change in adult users.

The label lists gynecomastia, frequent or prolonged erections, oligospermia at high doses, hirsutism, male-pattern baldness, seborrhea, acne, fluid and electrolyte retention, nausea, cholestatic jaundice and liver test changes. Cardiovascular events including myocardial infarction and stroke are listed, and post-marketing reports of venous thromboembolism are cited in the warnings.[3]

Testosterone is contraindicated in pregnancy because it can virilize a female fetus.[3] Older patients on androgens may have a higher risk of prostatic hypertrophy and prostate cancer, though the label says conclusive evidence is lacking.[3]

A network meta-analysis of 29 placebo-controlled randomized trials (3,393 men) found that every testosterone formulation raised hematocrit relative to placebo, with differences among routes; intramuscular esters including cypionate were among the larger increases.[12] A randomized trial compared hematocrit change with intranasal testosterone gel versus intramuscular testosterone cypionate in testosterone-deficient men.[13] A randomized pilot study examined 100 mg testosterone cypionate in trans men who had erythrocytosis.[14]

Laboratory work links testosterone to platelet changes: one study reported that testosterone increased thromboxane A2 receptor density and platelet aggregation responses in human platelets.[15] Rat studies of supraphysiologic cypionate and nandrolone reported effects on neuron counts in the locus coeruleus.[16] A 2024 case report described a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to cypionate injections.[17]

Wikipedia's overview lists common effects including acne, swelling, and breast enlargement in men from aromatization to estradiol, with mood changes, aggression, increased sex drive and reduced sperm production possible; reduced sperm production is described as reversible infertility.[9] Serious risks listed include liver toxicity, heart problems, blood clots and worsened sleep apnea.[9] The Anabolic steroid article adds that prolonged use temporarily shuts down natural testosterone production, that oligospermia, azoospermia and testicular atrophy can occur and are generally reversible, and that pattern baldness can be accelerated in men who are genetically predisposed.[18]

The TRAVERSE trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023, randomized 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with hypogonadism and existing or high cardiovascular risk to 1.62 percent transdermal testosterone gel or placebo. Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 7.0 percent on testosterone and 7.3 percent on placebo, meeting the noninferiority criterion, while atrial fibrillation, acute kidney injury and pulmonary embolism were more frequent in the testosterone group.[10] This was a gel trial in medically treated men, not cypionate injections or non-medical use. According to Wikipedia, the FDA stated in 2015 that benefits and safety for age-related low testosterone had not been established, and in February 2025 removed cardiovascular language from the boxed warning while adding a warning about increased blood pressure.[9]

The cypionate ester makes testosterone oil-soluble and slows its release from the injection depot. After conversion to free testosterone, it binds the androgen receptor and can also be converted to dihydrotestosterone (via 5-alpha-reductase) or estradiol (via aromatase).[1] Those downstream conversions are the reason hair loss, acne and gynecomastia appear on the adverse-effect list.[1][3]

Exogenous testosterone suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular axis, reducing the body's own luteinizing hormone-driven production; a randomized study from 1997 examined this suppression.[19]

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of roughly 7 to 8 days after intramuscular injection, which is why it is dosed far less often than short-acting preparations.[1] Subcutaneous administration has also been studied; Grokipedia describes pharmacokinetics similar to intramuscular injection in studies among transgender men.[2]
Testosterone cypionate is the cyclopentylpropionate ester of testosterone with the formula C27H40O3. It is a prodrug of testosterone and is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derivative.[1][2]

Testosterone was first isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939, according to Wikipedia.[9] Testosterone cypionate was synthesized and introduced for medical use in the United States in 1951, and it is now one of the most commonly used testosterone esters, alongside enanthate, undecanoate and propionate; it is marketed mainly in the United States.[1][1]

Wikipedia dates the drug's introduction to 1951 in the United States, under the Depo-Testosterone name.[1] Clinical use of long-acting esters in hypogonadism was established through the following decades, as summarised in a 1984 review.[7] Interest in its non-medical use grew with bodybuilding culture, and in the 2020s T Nation threads discuss prescription testosterone replacement providers, first cycle experiences and lab results at length.[20][11]

Anabolic-androgenic steroids spread through bodybuilding culture, and Wikipedia's overview of the class notes that media reports of so-called roid rage appeared from the mid-1980s onward. The US classified anabolic steroids as controlled substances under the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 1990.[9][18] Survey data cited there indicate that most non-medical users are non-competitive bodybuilders or non-athletes, with a median age around 25, who use the drugs for cosmetic reasons.[18]
It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the United States and Schedule IV in Canada, and requires a prescription in most jurisdictions.[1]

Wikipedia lists the UK as Class C, the EU as prescription-only, and testosterone as on the WHO Essential Medicines List; it is banned in competitive sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[9] Controlled status has fostered black markets selling smuggled, clandestinely made or counterfeit products, according to the Anabolic steroid article.[18]

subs.h: Use in physique and looks communities
paras: T Nation, a long-running strength and physique forum, hosts many threads on testosterone replacement therapy and non-medical use, covering provider choices, lab values and personal experiences.[20][11][21] On looksmaxxing forums, testosterone is discussed as a lever for jaw definition, facial hair, muscle and skin, and threads exist about sourcing; this article does not document sourcing or preparation.

Prescription testosterone replacement is a separate community topic from non-medical use. T Nation threads on TRT providers discuss clinics, lab monitoring and comparisons between injectable and other forms, while cycle threads discuss expected results for muscle, fat and skin.[20][11] Contributors to such threads frequently mention monitoring of hematocrit and estradiol, in line with the hematocrit findings described in the clinical literature.[20][12]

Testosterone replacement in older hypogonadal men: a 12-month randomized controlled trial assigned 15 hypogonadal men (mean age 68) to placebo and 17 (mean age 65) to testosterone, examining physical and cognitive decline over a year.[8]

Supraphysiologic dosing: a randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover trial in 56 men aged 20 to 50 gave testosterone cypionate for 6 weeks at doses rising to 600 mg per week, versus placebo, to evaluate manic and aggressive responses; it was designed because field studies of illicit steroid users had suggested mood effects.[5] An earlier study examined aggressive responding in male volunteers after gradually increasing doses.[22]
Route and hematocrit: a 2022 network meta-analysis of 29 randomized trials pooled formulations, and a 2023 randomized trial compared intranasal gel with intramuscular cypionate.[12][13]

Prostate cancer: bipolar androgen therapy alternates high and low testosterone in castration-resistant prostate cancer, with a pilot study published in 2015 and phase 2 follow-ups.[6][23] A 2026 JAMA Internal Medicine randomized trial examined testosterone in prostate cancer survivors with hypogonadism.[24]

Other: a randomized trial examined testosterone in infants with 47,XXY, and a phase 3 weekly auto-injector trial in hypogonadal men is registered.[25][26] No study was found evaluating testosterone cypionate for voice change or cosmetic goals in healthy people.

Muscle in healthy men: the 1996 randomized trial in 43 men found that testosterone enanthate increased muscle size and strength with or without training, and the largest gains occurred with training.[10] Cardiovascular safety: the 2023 TRAVERSE trial in 5,246 hypogonadal men found that gel testosterone was noninferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events.[10]

lore.intro: In physique and looks forums, testosterone cypionate is the most commonly discussed injectable androgen, covered in threads on prescribed replacement therapy and non-medical cycles.[20][11][21]

Its long half-life means infrequent injections maintain steady levels
Testosterone worsens hair loss and acne
Higher exposure causes mood changes and aggression
Blood thickening (high hematocrit) is a common side effect

Testosterone is safe for the heart when monitored

timeline.event: Testosterone is first isolated; it is approved for medical use in 1939.[9]
Introduced in the US as Depo-Testosterone.[1]
A review describes testosterone cypionate and enanthate as the long-acting injectable esters for adult male hypogonadism.[7]
Anabolic steroids are classified as controlled substances in the US under the Anabolic Steroid Control Act.[9]
New England Journal of Medicine trial of supraphysiologic testosterone in 43 healthy men reports gains in muscle size and strength.[10]
A 12-month randomized trial in older hypogonadal men is published.[8]
A randomized crossover trial examines supraphysiologic cypionate and mood.[5]
Pilot study of bipolar androgen therapy in prostate cancer published.[6]
Network meta-analysis compares hematocrit effects across testosterone routes.[12]
TRAVERSE trial in 5,246 hypogonadal men reports noninferiority for cardiovascular events with testosterone gel.[10]
FDA removes cardiovascular language from the testosterone boxed warning and adds a blood pressure warning.[9]
